job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with an AI assistant, honestly. I wake up in the room I share with my mate Sami in Glasgow, ask it to sort my applications by who's most likely to reply, and then I spend the morning on freelance work, mostly small business websites and a couple of chatbots. I send out maybe ten applications before lunch, then in the afternoon I fiddle with whatever gadget I'm building. It's busy, but it doesn't pay like a job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer engineering, passed, nothing flashy. My final project was a small drone that spots obstacles with a camera and a cheap board, and it worked about seven times out of ten, which my supervisor said was fine for a first attempt. I didn't have an internship, because I spent summer two working at a call centre to pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a little bit of a letdown, but honestly fine. At the pub I'd say the tools are useful and they're still just tools. Online I'd post a short thread on what actually works, to keep it honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the world I'm trying to break into stays the same, and my edge with the tools is smaller. If everyone is calm about AI, no one pays extra for someone who uses it all day. I'd be one of the many applicants with a pass degree, and I'd have to win on other things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the freelance work going and push it up to about six clients a month. I'd apply for jobs outside the usual graduate schemes, like small hardware startups and engineering firms near Glasgow. I'd also build a better portfolio, with the drone video on top, since it's the best thing I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated, to be honest, but not scared. It's more a feeling of slow going. The rent, the loan and the lack of a proper job still sit on top of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there'd be no extra pay for using AI all day. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every graduate can write a decent email or a script with a tool, it stops being special. It's like everyone knowing how to use a spreadsheet. So I'd need something else, like a physical project or real customers, to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the money work for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freelance brings in about four hundred in a good month and a hundred and fifty in a bad one. Sami and I split rent at six hundred, so I scrape through, and my loan repayments haven't started yet. When they do, I'll be properly squeezed.

say: I'd say it's a bit of a **letdown**, but the tools are still just tools.
Online I'd post a short honest thread on what actually works.
think: If everyone uses AI calmly, nobody pays **extra** for my daily use.
I'd have to win on other things, like projects and customers.
do: Push freelance clients up to about **six a month**.
Apply to small hardware startups and engineering firms near Glasgow.
Put the **drone video** at the top of my portfolio.
feel: A bit **deflated** but not scared: slow going.
Rent, loan and no proper job still sit on top.
S0.quote: If every graduate can write a decent email or a script with a tool, it stops being special.
fieldNote: He sees that his **AI skill** only matters if others lack it.
Loan repayments haven't started, which is a hidden pressure.
Cheerful tone, thin income of 150 to 400 pounds a month.

steps.text: Take on six paying freelance clients a month
Apply to small hardware startups around Glasgow
Film and post a better demo of the drone project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've been expecting, and people should get stuck in. Online I'd show how I've used the tools to do the work of a tiny agency. At the pub I'd say that anyone who isn't at least playing with them by now is behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the job I'd normally apply for, junior engineer or developer, gets scarcer, but I'm well placed to freelance. I'm at the point where I could present myself as a one-person team. The danger is that everyone else does the same, and then it's a race to the bottom on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a proper little business, with a name, invoices and three packages for small firms, like website, chatbot and monthly updates. I'd also take a cheap online course in hardware and robotics, since the robots will come to hands-on work and I want to be on that side. I'd keep applying as well, in case a good job pops up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good nerves, if that makes sense. I'm excited, but I can see the way it can go badly: a race to the bottom, and a bad month without clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from getting caught in a race to the bottom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having a niche. I'd aim at, say, small engineering and trades firms, who can't afford a developer but have a lot of paperwork. I'd learn their language, not just chase anyone with a website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the hardware and robotics course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the thinking side gets crowded fast, and I like making things you can touch. If robots reach hands-on work, someone has to install and fix them. I'd rather be the person who installs and fixes the robots than compete with a thousand other graduates writing code.

say: I'd say **get stuck in** and play with the tools.
Online I'd show how I do a tiny agency's work alone.
think: Junior developer jobs get scarcer, but I'm **well placed** to freelance.
The danger is a race to the bottom on price.
do: Set up a **proper little business** with three packages for small firms.
Take a cheap online course in hardware and robotics.
Aim at engineering and **trades firms** with lots of paperwork.
feel: **Good nerves**: excited, but I see how it could go badly.
Wary of a bad month without clients.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who installs and fixes the robots than compete with a thousand other graduates writing code.
fieldNote: He moves **early** and treats disruption as an opening, as an adaptive person does.
Has a niche idea: small engineering and trades firms.
Mood stays anxious because freelance income is still small and uneven.

steps.text: Register a small business and set up invoicing
Sell website and chatbot packages to small trades firms
Take an online course in robotics and hardware
Keep applying for engineering jobs in Glasgow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a huge shock, so we should be loud about it. Online I'd post plain explanations for people who don't follow the news, and I'd ask the government for a plan. At the pub I'd say get your money sorted now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels like my entire field disappears in two years. The company I'd work for wouldn't hire me because AI would do the thinking part for nothing. The only bit that would last is the hands-on side, and robots for that arrive only three years later, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the hands-on side immediately: electronics repair, installing solar and smart meters, anything with a toolbox. I'd also try to build one thing that sells, a product I can make with my own hands. And I'd cut every cost, including my phone plan, then ask Sami whether we can find a cheaper room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but weirdly awake. I'd feel I had to move now or I'd be stuck. I don't think I'd freeze, which surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the product be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a small sensor kit, like a damp or temperature sensor for rental homes, sold to landlords and tenants. It uses what I know, but it's physical and local. If it worked I could sell through a local hardware shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They live in the Alps, and my mum worries easily. I'd say I've got a plan, I'm working, and I've got savings coming. I'd probably exaggerate a little, because she can't help from there and I don't want her up at night.

say: I'd say it's a **huge shock** and we should be loud about it.
Online I'd post plain explanations and ask for a government plan.
think: My whole field **disappears** in two years.
Only the hands-on side lasts, until robots reach it around 2031.
do: Switch to **hands-on work**: electronics repair, solar installs, smart meters.
Build one small product I can make myself and sell locally.
Cut costs and look for a **cheaper room** with Sami.
S2.quote: I'd feel I had to move now or I'd be stuck. I don't think I'd freeze, which surprises me.
fieldNote: Panics less than expected: an **adaptive** reflex turns fear into movement.
Hands-on pivot is directly tied to the three-year robot delay.
Hides worry from his mother, who lives abroad.

steps.text: Apply for solar installer and electronics repair jobs
Build and sell a small sensor kit to local landlords
Cancel the phone plan and subscriptions
Ask Sami about moving to a cheaper room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we've got a window. I'd tell friends to build skills that still matter and get a bit of money together. Online I'd keep posting practical stuff, because people respond to that more than doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is enough for me to make a decent start. I could get a first job, then start a small firm on the side, and by 2031 I'd have a record and some cash. I'd say it's a good bet for someone like me, because I'm quick to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first engineering or technical job that lets me work on real hardware. I'd keep the freelance work going on weekends. I'd put aside two hundred a month and spend a little on a good second-hand 3D printer, because I'd want to make physical stuff, since that lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly upbeat, with a worry in the background. I'd feel like I'd been given a chance. I'm just not sure whether I'd use it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a 3D printer in the middle of all that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's an investment that gives something back. I could print parts for my sensor kits and sell them. And when thinking work goes to AI, someone who can design and make things has more choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first year than in the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more. In two years I'd save everything and run lean. With five I can afford to buy a printer, take a short course and still keep a cushion. It's a more stretched-out kind of risk.

say: I'd say there's **a window** and we should build skills that still matter.
Online I'd keep posting practical advice, not doom.
think: Five years is enough for a **decent start**: a first job, a side firm and a record.
I'm quick to try things, which suits this timeline.
do: Take the first technical job with **real hardware**.
Keep freelance going at weekends and save **two hundred** a month.
Buy a second-hand 3D printer to make parts.
feel: Mostly **upbeat**, with a worry in the background.
Unsure whether I'd use the chance well.
S3.quote: When thinking work goes to AI, someone who can design and make things has more choice.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **spend** on a printer and a course; two years would not.
Mood drops to uneasy because he sees a workable path.
Admits self-doubt about using the window well.

steps.text: Take the first technical job working with real hardware
Sell printed parts and sensor kits at weekends
Put two hundred pounds a month into savings
Buy a second-hand 3D printer for small production

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway, and the best advice is to use it. At the pub I'd say a decade's enough to change plans two or three times. Online I'd keep sharing the things I build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is the one where I'd have fun and still be fine. I'd be thirty-three in 2036 and could have a business, a small team and a decent career behind me. If AGI shows up, I'd already be the one who runs the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a good job, learn a lot in three years, then use that to start something of my own. I'd study part-time in robotics or machine design if someone paid for half. I'd save aggressively for a deposit on a small place, because I'd want something solid before things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and actually excited. It's the first picture where I imagine the good version of my life, and I'm in it. I don't feel afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of that picture you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The middle years, say 2031 to 2034. That's when thinking AI is everywhere and robots are close. If my business only does thinking work, it'd be at risk, so I'd need to have shifted toward physical stuff by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone your age who's more worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get one real skill with your hands and one with software. Don't pick between them. And use the tools every day, because nobody's going to hand you a job just for knowing they exist.

say: I'd say it's a long runway, so **use it**.
A decade is enough to change plans two or three times.
think: Ten years is the one where I'd have **fun** and still be fine.
By 2036 I could have a business, a small team and a career behind me.
do: Start with a **good job**, learn for three years, then start my own firm.
Study part-time in robotics or **machine design** if someone pays half.
Save hard for a deposit on a small place.
feel: The first picture where I imagine the good version of my life.
S4.quote: I'd say get one real skill with your hands and one with software. Don't pick between them.
fieldNote: Only here does he feel **calm**, since ten years allows a real business and a deposit.
Names the risky middle years, 2031 to 2034, and plans a physical shift.
Advice to peers is concrete and practical.

steps.text: Take a good engineering job and stay three years
Study part-time robotics or machine design
Save for a deposit on a small flat
Start my own small hardware and software firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be starting with nothing and the whole field would be gone. It would hurt in a specific way: I'd have built all the right skills and still be late. What would help is cheap, quick retraining in hands-on work, and a way for people like me to start a small business without being buried in loan repayments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as cheerful as I sound. People think the ones who use the tools are fine, and mostly we're just early to worry. I joke a lot, but I do the sums at night, like everyone else.

headlineQuote: I'm not as cheerful as I sound. People think the ones who use the tools are fine, and mostly we're just early to worry.
portrait: **Umar**, 23, passed computer engineering without an internship and shares a rented room in Glasgow with his friend Sami.
He earns **150 to 400 pounds** a month freelancing on small websites and chatbots, and his loan repayments haven't started.
Centrist and curious, he uses AI every day, takes risks and moves early.
When disruption is sharp he swings to hands-on work: solar installs, a sensor kit and a 3D printer.
His mood runs from anxious to alarmed in the two-year world and calm only in the ten-year one.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries him most: he'd start from nothing and be late.
He worries the skills he built would arrive too late.
whatWouldHelp: A way to start a small business without being buried by loan repayments.
